units.title: Unit 25 — Cooking
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 56–57 (PDF pages 57–58).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Distinguish boiling, frying, grilling, roasting, baking and barbecuing, and name the equipment used.
Give simple cooking instructions using peel, chop, add, stir and taste.
Describe food using taste, flavour, tasty, spicy, sour, bitter, smooth and delicious.
Talk about ingredients, recipes and dishes with natural food-preparation collocations.
Use cook, cooker, a good cook, good at cooking and make a dish accurately.

items.example: Boil the potatoes for fifteen minutes.
items.note: Cook food in boiling water; also used for heating water.

items.example: Fry the onions gently in a little oil.
items.note: Cook food in hot oil or fat, usually in a pan.

items.example: Grill the fish until it is cooked through.
items.note: In British English, grilling often means cooking under direct heat.

items.example: We often roast chicken for Sunday lunch.
items.note: Cook in an oven, traditionally with fat or oil, particularly meat.

items.pt: assar no forno (pães, bolos e massas)
items.example: She is going to bake a chocolate cake.
items.note: Cook in an oven, especially bread, cakes, pies or potatoes.

items.example: They barbecue vegetables and fish in the summer.
items.note: Cook over an open fire or outdoor grill.

items.example: This dish contains raw vegetables.
items.note: Not cooked; contrasts with boiled, fried and roasted.

items.example: Heat the sauce in a small saucepan.
items.note: A deep pan with a long handle, often used for boiling.

items.example: Put a little oil in the frying pan.
items.note: A wide, shallow pan for frying food.

items.pt: grelha; parte do forno para grelhar
items.example: Place the toast under the grill.
items.note: British English: equipment producing strong heat from above.

items.example: The bread is still in the oven.
items.note: An enclosed appliance for roasting and baking food.

items.example: We bought a small barbecue for the garden.
items.note: An outdoor cooking device; can also mean an outdoor meal.

items.example: We served boiled potatoes with the fish.
items.note: Boiled describes food cooked in water.

items.example: We made fried rice with leftover vegetables.
items.note: Fried is the past participle used as an adjective.

items.example: The restaurant serves roast beef on Sundays.
items.note: Roast can be used before a noun to describe the cooking method.

items.example: I had a baked potato with cheese for lunch.
items.note: A potato cooked in the oven, often with its skin.

items.pt: frango feito na churrasqueira; frango grelhado
items.example: We ate barbecued chicken at the family lunch.
items.note: Barbecued is the participle used before the food.

items.example: Peel the carrots before cutting them.
items.note: Remove the outer skin of fruit or vegetables.

items.example: The skin of these potatoes is very thin.
items.note: The outer covering removed when you peel something.

items.example: Chop the onion into small pieces.
items.note: Cut food into small pieces using a knife.

items.example: Add the chopped tomatoes to the pan.
items.note: Chopped is the past participle of chop used as an adjective.

items.example: Add some water if the sauce is too thick.
items.note: Put an ingredient together with the others; often add something to something.

items.example: Add the garlic to the tomatoes.
items.note: Add + ingredient + to + dish or mixture.

items.example: Stir the soup for two minutes.
items.note: Move food around in a pan or bowl using a spoon.

items.example: I prepare the vegetables before I start cooking.
items.note: Prepare means get food ready to be cooked or served.

items.example: The chef prepares fresh pasta every morning.
items.note: Someone whose job is cooking food, often in a restaurant.

items.example: Taste the sauce before serving it.
items.note: Put a small amount in your mouth to check its flavour.

items.example: I love the taste of fresh strawberries.
items.note: The flavour you experience when you eat or drink.

items.example: The soup tasted strange after I added the spice.
items.note: Taste + adjective describes the flavour of food.

items.example: That vegetable pie was really tasty.
items.note: Adjective meaning having a pleasant flavour; not tasteful.

items.example: This curry is too spicy for me.
items.note: Describes food with a strong, hot flavour.

items.example: Which flavour of ice cream would you like?
items.note: British spelling: flavour. Used to identify or describe a particular taste.

items.example: They sell yoghurt in several different flavours.
items.note: Use flavours rather than tastes for different varieties of a product.

items.example: The burnt sauce tasted horrible.
items.note: Strong adjective for something very unpleasant; opposite in this context: delicious.

items.example: The freshly baked bread was delicious.
items.note: Very pleasant to taste; stronger than good or tasty.

items.example: These lemons are extremely sour.
items.note: Typical taste of lemons; contrasted with sweet.

items.example: The strawberries are sweet enough without sugar.
items.note: Food containing sugar or having a sugary taste; contrasts with sour.

items.example: I prefer dark, bitter chocolate.
items.note: Sharp, sometimes unpleasant taste, but not always a negative description.

items.example: This coffee has a rich, smooth flavour.
items.note: For coffee, smooth suggests a pleasant, less harsh taste.

items.example: She prefers strong coffee without milk.
items.note: Strong describes the intensity of coffee flavour.

items.pt: chocolate amargo; chocolate com alto teor de cacau
items.example: A piece of dark chocolate goes well with coffee.
items.note: Often has a more bitter taste than milk chocolate.

items.example: He ordered chocolate-flavoured ice cream.
items.note: The -flavoured adjective describes which flavour a product has.

items.example: I followed a recipe from a cooking website.
items.note: Instructions explaining how to prepare a particular dish.

items.example: It is easier to follow a recipe the first time.
items.note: Use follow, not make, for using recipe instructions.

items.example: Garlic is an important ingredient in this dish.
items.note: One of the foods used to prepare a meal; often plural: ingredients.

items.example: Make sure the oven is hot before baking.
items.note: Check or arrange that something is definitely true.

items.example: We shared a vegetable pie for dinner.
items.note: An enclosed or open pastry dish, often sweet or savoury.

items.example: My grandmother makes a lovely apple pie.
items.note: A sweet pie containing apples.

items.example: My father is a good cook.
items.note: Use cook for a person who cooks; cooker names the equipment.

items.example: We replaced the old cooker last month.
items.note: British English noun for an appliance used to cook food, not a person.

items.pt: ser bom em cozinhar; cozinhar bem
items.example: She is very good at cooking fish.
items.note: Use good at + -ing, not good in cooking.

items.example: We often cook vegetables in the evening.
items.note: Use cook when discussing the action or the type of food.

items.pt: preparar um prato; fazer uma receita
items.example: I am going to make a pasta dish for lunch.
items.note: Use make when referring to preparing a complete dish or meal.

items.example: I offered to make dessert for our guests.
items.note: Natural expression for preparing a dessert.

items.pt: um pouco nervoso; um pouco apreensivo
items.example: I feel a bit nervous when I cook for visitors.
items.note: A bit softens the description of how someone feels.

sectionsChecked: A: Ways of cooking food; pictures of kitchen equipment
C: What does it taste like?; Language help on sour, sweet, bitter and smooth
D: Are you a good cook?; Common mistakes on cook/cooker and cook/make

units.title: Unit 26 — City life
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 58–59 (PDF pages 59–60).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Describe rush-hour journeys, parking problems, traffic jams and travel-related stress.
Use natural contrasts between stressful situations and stressed or exhausted people.
Talk about nightlife, town centres and cultural activities in a city.
Discuss advantages and disadvantages, safety, pollution and crime in urban areas.
Express value for money and describe lively, crowded or dull places.

items.example: The roads are crowded during the morning rush hour.
items.note: The time when many people travel to or from work.

items.example: The station is very busy at eight in the morning.
items.note: Used for crowded places or times with much activity.

items.example: I was in a hurry and left my umbrella at home.
items.note: An expression for wanting to do something quickly.

items.pt: ficar preso; ficar impedido de avançar
items.example: We got stuck in the lift for ten minutes.
items.note: Become unable to move or continue.

items.word: get stuck in a traffic jam
items.example: We got stuck in a traffic jam on our way home.
items.note: Common verb pattern: get stuck in traffic or in a traffic jam.

items.example: A traffic jam delayed our journey.
items.note: A long line of vehicles moving very slowly or not moving.

items.example: You cannot park outside the hospital.
items.note: Leave a vehicle in a particular place.

items.example: There was nowhere to park near the office.
items.note: Use nowhere to park for a lack of available parking.

items.example: The car park behind the hotel is free.
items.note: British English noun for a parking area; American English: parking lot.

items.example: I found a parking space near the entrance.
items.note: A single place for one vehicle; not a parking.

items.example: The car park was full by half past eight.
items.note: Describes a place with no more room or available capacity.

items.example: I get the bus to work twice a week.
items.note: British English informal way to say travel by bus.

items.example: My journey to work takes forty minutes.
items.note: A journey is travel from one place to another.

items.example: It takes longer to get home by bus.
items.note: Use it takes longer + to-infinitive for increased duration.

items.example: Driving in heavy traffic can be stressful.
items.note: Describes a situation that causes stress, not the person experiencing it.

items.example: I felt stressed after the long commute.
items.note: Describes a person experiencing stress; compare stressful.

items.example: I was exhausted when I finally got home.
items.note: Very tired; stronger than tired.

items.example: The city has excellent nightlife at weekends.
items.note: Evening and night-time social activities and entertainment.

items.example: One advantage of living here is the public transport.
items.note: A positive feature of a situation; compare disadvantage.

items.example: The town centre is busy on Friday evenings.
items.note: British English expression for the central area with shops and services.

items.example: The square is lively in the evenings.
items.note: Full of people, activity and excitement; opposite in context: dull.

items.example: There is a wide variety of restaurants near the square.
items.note: Use a wide variety of + plural noun or uncountable noun.

items.example: The city is known for its music and culture.
items.note: Includes artistic activities and a community’s traditions.

items.example: The festival is an important cultural event.
items.note: Adjective formed from culture.

items.example: There are many cultural activities for children.
items.note: Activities such as concerts, theatre, cinema and exhibitions.

items.example: We went to the cinema after dinner.
items.note: British English: go to the cinema, often go to the movies in US English.

items.example: There is a small theatre near the station.
items.note: British English spelling: theatre; American English: theater.

items.example: We attended a concert in the city centre.
items.note: A live public performance of music.

items.example: The art gallery has a new exhibition.
items.note: A building or room where art is displayed.

items.example: The main disadvantage is the cost of housing.
items.note: A negative feature or problem; opposite: advantage.

items.example: The streets get crowded before the football match.
items.note: Having many people in a small space; opposite in the source: quiet.

items.example: The neighbourhood is quiet after ten o’clock.
items.note: With little noise or activity; contrasts with crowded or lively in context.

items.example: The river became dirty after the storm.
items.note: Not clean; one possible problem in cities.

items.example: The streets are clean and well maintained.
items.note: Opposite of dirty.

items.example: Cycling on this busy road can be dangerous.
items.note: Not safe; used for places or activities that may cause harm.

items.example: I feel safe walking here during the day.
items.note: Not dangerous; opposite of dangerous.

items.example: Traffic causes a lot of air pollution in the city.
items.note: Harmful substances in air, water or the environment.

items.pt: índice de criminalidade; taxa de crimes
items.example: The crime rate has fallen in recent years.
items.note: The amount of crime in a place during a period.

items.example: The square is well lit at night.
items.note: At night is idiomatic; do not confuse it with in the evening.

items.example: I do not like walking home on my own after midnight.
items.note: On my own means alone; can change the possessive: on her own.

items.example: We decided to get a taxi home.
items.note: Common everyday expression for travelling by taxi.

items.example: Flats in the city centre are expensive.
items.note: Having a high price; opposite: cheap.

items.example: They rent a flat near the station.
items.note: British English: flat; often apartment in American English.

items.pt: custo-benefício; relação entre qualidade e preço
items.example: This small café offers excellent value for money.
items.note: How good or useful something is compared with its price.

items.pt: bom custo-benefício; vale o preço pago
items.example: The cheaper flat is good value for money.
items.note: Describes something worth its price.

items.example: On the positive side, the station is very close.
items.note: Introduces a benefit after mentioning drawbacks.

items.pt: uma mistura; uma diversidade de pessoas
items.example: The neighbourhood has a mix of people from different countries.
items.note: Mix refers to different kinds of people or things together.

items.example: The city has residents of many nationalities.
items.note: A person’s national identity; plural: nationalities.

items.example: There is always something going on in the town centre.
items.note: Go on means happen; used for events and activities.

items.example: The village felt dull after dark.
items.note: Not exciting or interesting; opposite: exciting or lively.

items.example: Moving to a new city can be exciting.
items.note: Causing interest and enthusiasm; opposite: dull.

items.example: There was nowhere to sit on the crowded train.
items.note: No place is available or exists.

items.example: Many cities are working to reduce poverty.
items.note: The state of being very poor; an exercise-only vocabulary target.

sectionsChecked: A: The rush hour; Common mistakes on stressed/stressful and car park/parking space
B: The nightlife; photograph and cultural activities
